truth:
Octopuses have three hearts. Two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills, while a systemic heart circulates it through the rest of the body. The systemic heart slows or stops when the octopus swims, which is one reason they prefer crawling to sustained swimming. Their blood uses hemocyanin, a copper-based protein that carries oxygen efficiently in cold, low-oxygen seawater.

About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons sit in its arms rather than its central brain. Each arm can taste, touch, and make local decisions. Researchers have observed severed arms reaching for food and grasping objects. This distributed design differs sharply from the centralized control found in vertebrate nervous systems.

Octopuses change color and texture in a fraction of a second using chromatophores, small pigment sacs that muscles stretch open or squeeze shut. Beneath them lie iridophores that reflect light and leucophores that scatter it, giving the animal control over brightness as well as hue. How they match backgrounds so precisely is still debated, though light-sensitive proteins in the skin may contribute.

When threatened, many octopuses release a cloud of ink from a sac near the funnel. The ink contains melanin and mucus, and it may also interfere with a predator's chemical senses. The cloud works as a visual decoy, letting the octopus slip away while the predator focuses on the dark shape. Some species also leave a false body outline in the ink as an extra distraction.

Octopuses are famous escape artists. Giant Pacific octopuses have been recorded squeezing through openings no wider than their beak, the one hard part of their body. They can also unscrew jar lids, climb out of tanks, and slip through drains. Aquarium keepers therefore secure lids and cover gaps. Their soft bodies make the escape possible, and their intelligence makes it deliberate.

Most octopus species live only one to two years, and many die shortly after breeding. Females lay thousands of eggs and often tend them for months without eating. Their health declines rapidly after the eggs hatch. In laboratory studies, removing the optic glands from females has been reported to extend their lives and trigger egg-laying, suggesting hormones from those glands drive this decline.
